raw_response:
I am a 74-year-old woman who has farmed these fields for 35 years. I never went to school, so I don't read books about farming—I read the land, the sky, and what my neighbors do. My farm is only 5 mu, and there are just two of us at home now. My son works off-farm in the city, sending back a little money when he can, but he can't help in the fields. So it's mostly me, and my back isn't what it used to be.

This year I'll keep my 3 mu of spring maize and 2 mu of cotton, same as last year. I thought about giving up the cotton—bending down to pick it three, four times gets harder every autumn—but Lao Zhang down the road said the cotton price at the buying station was decent last year, and I need that cash for medicine and daily expenses. The maize is easier; I can hire a small combine to harvest it, and it feeds us and the chickens.

For the maize, I'll plant around April 20th when the soil feels warm enough. I buy hybrid seed from the agricultural shop in town—one small bag per mu, costs about 40 yuan. Before planting, I spread half a big bag of that compound fertilizer—the kind with the three numbers I can't read, but the shopkeeper says it's good—into the furrows. That's my base. When the maize is knee-high, around June, I topdress with another half-bag of urea. Last year I put more fertilizer and the stalks grew tall but the ears didn't fill any better, so I won't waste that money again. I irrigate twice if it's dry—once when it's jointing, once when the tassels come out. The well water costs electricity, so if it rains I thank heaven and keep the pump off.

The cotton goes in around the same time, late April. I bought new seed this year because my saved seed from last year didn't sprout well—only about half came up, and I had to replant. For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer at planting, and when the cotton starts flowering in July I add some urea along the rows. Cotton needs more watching for bugs. I hire the spray drone fellow for herbicide, and if I see bollworms or aphids—I remember two years ago the aphids were terrible—I spray. I'll irrigate the cotton twice, at flowering and when the bolls are filling.

Labor is what worries me most. For the maize, I can manage the planting and weeding myself, and hire a combine for harvest—that's two days of hired help. But cotton picking is all by hand. Last year I hired two women from the village to help pick, paid them by the jin. It cost me but without them the cotton would have stayed in the field. I'll need to hire help again, maybe six days altogether for the cotton. I hate spending that money, but I hate the thought of losing the crop more.

I figure all my costs—seed, fertilizer, pesticide, electricity for the pump, and hired labor—will come to about 1,800 yuan. That's a lot for us. I have to be careful. I expect about 450 kg of maize per mu if the weather is normal, and around 250 kg of seed cotton per mu. I'm not trying to get rich. I just want to get through the year, pay for my blood pressure medicine, and have enough left to eat.
